Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Mr. Nguyen is a 42-year-old South Eastern Asian man who lives with his wife and children on their family farm in rural America. His life took a dramatic turn when his youngest child, a vibrant toddler, was diagnosed with a severe illness that threatened her life. The memory of the hospital stay and the fear he experienced during those critical days has left deep scars. At night, under the dim light of his farmhouse, Mr. Nguyen is often haunted by the sounds of machines beeping and doctors rushing around, the same sensations he felt when he held his child's tiny hand in the ICU. Since that traumatic event, certain triggers have become particularly potent for him. The sound of an ambulance siren or a song played during those hospital days can suddenly bring back vivid memories of the trauma. When these moments occur, Mr. Nguyen feels as if he is right back in the hospital, reliving the fear and helplessness all over again. These sudden fragments of memory feel so present that they disrupt his daily life, leaving him feeling disoriented and anxious. To cope with this overwhelming anxiety, Mr. Nguyen has developed several maladaptive strategies. He often stays up until very late at night to avoid the darkness and quiet of his home, which he associates with the frightening memories of the hospital nights. Lying in bed or falling asleep triggers intense flashbacks, so he avoids sleep by keeping himself busy with farm chores well into the evening. This pattern has become a cycle, where the fear of these memories keeps him awake, but staying up late only exacerbates his anxiety and makes the next night even more difficult. Mr. Nguyen also finds himself avoiding other people, particularly those who remind him of the hospital staff or the doctors he encountered during that time. His relationships have been strained as a result; he has become increasingly isolated from friends and family. This avoidance behavior is not just about preventing reminders but also about managing his intense anxiety. Each encounter with someone who reminds him of that period triggers another wave of distress, reinforcing the cycle. The night holds particular terror for Mr. Nguyen. The darkness seems to amplify every sound and memory, making it feel as if he’s back in the hospital, surrounded by beeping machines and the sterile smell of antiseptic. Even the act of lying down or closing his eyes can precipitate a flashback. As a result, he often sits up late into the night, engaging in repetitive tasks like checking and rechecking farm equipment to keep himself occupied and distracted from these intrusive thoughts. The memory fragments are particularly disruptive when they appear suddenly without warning during the day. For example, a specific song might play on the radio while he is driving his tractor, transporting him back to those harrowing moments. The reliving of the event leaves him feeling shaken and disoriented, sometimes leading him to abruptly end his tasks and isolate himself further. What frightens Mr. Nguyen most is the fear that these memories will never go away and that he will continue to be trapped in this cycle of anxiety and avoidance forever. He recognizes that his behavior has been affecting his work and relationships, but he feels helpless to change it. The memory fragments keep him on edge, perpetuating the pattern of maladaptive strategies. Mr. Nguyen’s current state is marked by a growing sense of desperation and isolation. His wife has noticed his increasing withdrawal and urged him to seek help. While he is hesitant about opening up to someone else, he hopes that with support, he can find a way to manage these overwhelming memories and triggers, regain control over his life, and reconnect with the family and farm he loves. The experience of reliving those traumatic moments has made Mr. Nguyen certain that he will never truly be free from the pain and fear associated with his child’s illness. Despite this, he is finally seeking help because he realizes that the cycle must break for him to reclaim a sense of normalcy in his life.
